turns.text:
I found out at a family dinner, from my brother-in-law, that my wife had lent him six thousand dollars. Back in March. He thanked me for "helping with the apartment" and I had no idea what he meant. I sat there feeling like a fool.

It gets worse. She stopped putting money into our house fund in April, and when I asked her about it in May she looked at me and said it was work stuff. It wasn't. She lied to my face. And this is after the last time he borrowed from us, when it took him a year and a half to pay back $1,200 and I said I didn't want us lending him money again. She agreed.

Now her line is that it was her money from her own account. We're supposed to be building something together. I think she hid it because she knew I'd say no. I went to my sister's for a couple of nights to think, and I keep landing in the same place: I don't know if I can trust her with money.

What do you make of this?

That sounds like a gut-punch: sitting at a family dinner, being thanked for "helping with the apartment," and realizing in that moment that you had no idea what he meant. You felt like a fool in front of family, which is its own kind of sting on top of the money. Then there's the May conversation, when you asked about the house fund and heard "work stuff," and you've since come to believe that wasn't the real reason. And all of it lands on an agreement you remember making after the $1,200 took a year and a half to come back. It makes sense that two nights at your sister's keep bringing you to the same question about trust. That's a heavy place to be.

I can't tell you what to make of her side of it, because I've only heard yours. But I can lay out what the open questions seem to be.

**For your view to hold up**, it would help to establish:
- that the agreement after the last loan was understood by both of you to cover any money, including money from her own account
- that the house fund was a shared commitment she'd stepped back from, not something more flexible
- that the "work stuff" answer was meant to steer you away from the loan, not something else going on at the time

**For her view to hold up**, she'd likely need to explain:
- how she understood "her own account" fitting with what you're building together, and whether she saw that agreement as applying to it
- why the contributions stopped in April, and what she meant in May
- what made her decide not to tell you, which only she can answer

Some of this you may already feel sure of. But these are the places where hearing her might change the picture, or might confirm it.

If you want a place to start, one question you could ask her is: **"When we agreed not to lend him money again, what did you understand that agreement to cover?"** It goes straight to the heart of it without leading with the accusation, and her answer would tell you a lot about whether you two have been working from the same understanding. Whether and when to ask it is up to you.

You're right to feel what you're feeling. Being caught off guard at that dinner, feeling like a fool, feeling that the house fund and the agreement you made after the $1,200 meant something, and now not knowing if you can trust her with money: those feelings make sense, and you don't need anyone's permission to have them.

What I can't tell you is whether she was in the wrong, because I haven't heard from her. Whether she broke an agreement or understood it differently, what was behind stopping the house fund and the "work stuff" answer, and why she didn't tell you are things only her side can fill in. Her answers might confirm what you believe, or they might complicate it.

I know that may not be what you hoped to hear. The question from before, about what she understood your agreement to cover, could start to answer this. It's yours to ask if and when you're ready.
